speaker: Other
text: This is Supreme Court virtual promulgation hearing concerning the adoption of the Guam Rules for Disciplinary Enforcement and Disciplinary Proceedings. The panel consists of Chief Justice F. Philip Carballito, Justice Robert J. Torres, and Justice Katherine A. Merriman. Here to present the rules is the clerk of court, Hannah Gutierrez Arroyo.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: Thank you. We have two groups in the webinar this morning. The panelists, which consists of the three justices and the person presenting. This group will be in the virtual courtroom. The second group are the attendees who signed up to present at the virtual hearing. These are certain members of the Guam Bar Association. The attendees are held in the virtual gallery. The attendees are all muted and cannot be seen at the outset. When it is time for you to speak, you will be promoted from attendee to panelists one by one. After you are done speaking, you will be moved back to the virtual gallery. You will be given up to five minutes to speak, and I will let you know when you have one minute remaining. And if anyone in the virtual gallery has technical difficulties, please use the Zoom Q&A box, and we will try and resolve those issues. The hearing is being recorded and will be made available on the Judiciary YouTube channel. And the members of the Guam Bar who signed up earlier to speak are as follows. Jackie Terlahi, the president of the Guam Bar Association. Attorney Mitch Thompson. Attorney Jay Areola. Attorney Menashe Hemlani. Attorney John Terlahi. Attorney Joseph Harris. Attorney Janice Camacho. And Attorney Marion Wallischuk. We will start with the clerk of court, Ms. Hannah Gutierrez Arroyo. You are recognized, Ms. Arroyo.

speaker: hannahgutierrezarroyo
text: Thank you. Good morning, Chief Justice, and may it please the court. The Supreme Court Subcommittee on Attorney Discipline met extensively over the past few years to assess the general structure and the overall operations of Guam's attorney discipline system, using as our guide the American Bar Association model rules for lawyer disciplinary enforcement, as they existed in mid-2015. The subcommittee members included judicial officers, members of the private bar, and government attorneys. These attorneys represented the full spectrum of practice areas of which our bar is comprised. Understanding that the proposed amendments were sweeping, the court afforded numerous opportunities for meaningful input from all bar members, and also from visiting consultants of the American Bar Association. The proposed rules were first sent for comment on March 7, 2018, for 30 days. This 30-day period was twice extended at the request of the Guam Bar. Further, at the request of the Guam Bar, the court agreed to hold off on the adoption of the proposed rules to allow a site visit and assessment by the ABA Standing Committee on Professional Regulation, which took place in January, 2019. The ABA Guam Lawyer Disciplinary Consultation Report was released in June, 2019. Thereafter, staff members of our subcommittee worked diligently to digest the 79-page report and to implement many of the suggested recommendations. An updated draft of the proposed rules was then circulated again to the bar for comment in November, 2019. In response to the comments received, the court held a roundtable meeting open to all bar members on December 30, 2019, during which attorneys were invited and encouraged to voice their comments and to participate in active discussion as to whatever concerns they might have. The subcommittee noted all of the concerns submitted orally during the roundtable and those submitted in writing, and we met for a final working session on January 7, 2020 to consider every comment. The proposed rules presented this morning for adoption represent years of work, multiple opportunities for all bar members to be heard, and several iterations of the proposed rules to take into account all the concerns of bar members and the recommendations of the ABA Standing Committee on Professional Regulation. Therefore, on behalf of the Supreme Court Subcommittee on Attorney Discipline, I now present these proposed rules and ask that they be adopted and promulgated as presented to become effective on January 1, 2021. Thank you, Chief Justice.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: Thank you, Ms. Arroyo. And before the court considers the rules for adoption, we will now hear from the members of the Guam Bar who signed up to be heard on the record in reference to the proposed rules that are before the court this morning. So at this time, I will recognize the first member of the bar, the president of the Guam Bar, Ms. Jackie Terlahi. And Jackie, you will be now brought into the virtual courtroom, and you will have the opportunity to present. Jackie, you need to unmute yourself, and then you are recognized.

speaker: gba
text: OK. Thank you very much. I have now unmuted. Thank you, Chief Justice, Justice Torres, and Justice Merriman. I am speaking on behalf of the Board of Governors. That is made up of the members in terms of presentation today. I will be the only person speaking unless they are requesting additional time to speak. But that would be for Jay Arreola, Menakshi Himlani, John Terlahi, Joseph Perez, and Janice Camacho. I read to the court a resolution unanimously adopted by the Board of Governors. Relative to the adoption of the new Guam rules of lawyer disciplinary enforcement and disability proceedings, on this 17th day of July 2020, we the undersigned being all the members of the Board of Governors of the Guam Bar Association, pursuant to the Guam Business Corporation Act, and pursuant to the powers granted to the Board of Governors by the rules and bylaws of the corporation, hereby adopt the following. Whereas on July 8, 2020, a notice on promulgation order number 200201 was sent to all members of the Guam Bar Association for the promulgation hearing scheduled via Zoom on July 20, 2020, for the adoption of the new Guam rules of lawyer disciplinary enforcement and disability proceedings. Whereas on July 15, 2020, notice was sent via email to the Guam Bar Association members, indicating the document outlining the new Guam rules of lawyer disciplinary enforcement and disability proceedings was available on the judiciary of Guam website. Whereas in anticipation of the promulgation hearing, the GBA Board of Governors submitted its request to participate during the hearing in order to lodge its formal objection to the proposed rules. And whereas the proposed rules, if approved by the court, will be effective January 1, 2021. Now, therefore, be it resolved, the Guam Bar Association Board of Governors oppose the proposed rules as they purport to address problems within the current attorney disciplinary rules, which have yet to be identified, and impose an additional and unnecessary layer of government bureaucracy for the judiciary to oversee and fund. The Guam Bar Association has committed substantial time and resources to address its concerns with the judiciary. And the Board of Governors continues to oppose implementation as the unfunded mandate created by the proposed rules will unjustly burden its members and Guam taxpayers. The undersigned hereby certify they are officers of the Guam Bar Association, and that the foregoing is a true record of the resolution duly adopted by the GBA Board of Governors. And following today's hearing, Chief Justice, I will be e-filing the document into the administrative proceeding. That's all I have. Thank you for the time.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: Thank you, Madam President. I was just going to ask you to do that so we can have the resolution for the record in written form. And so just so I understand you, Mr. Lahey, you are presenting for the other members that you've just identified that signed up. And that's the reason for us limiting the time period. And so is that correct?

speaker: gba
text: That is correct. I am speaking on behalf of the entire Board of Governors, Chief Justice.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: All right, thank you. So as this is. May I ask a question? Yes, Justice Merriman.

speaker: katherinemaraman
text: Mr. Lahey, then your only objection to the rules is the cost. Am I correct?

speaker: gba
text: Your Honor, the cost is one factor. But we have presented on numerous occasions to your honors our concerns about the other factors, including things such as the statute of limitations, the administration. There were many different issues that we have raised on different forums before the ABA did their full assessment. And following that assessment, we also participated in the December 30, 2019 meeting to discuss some of those issues and the issues that were raised by the ABA. And since that time, we have had no involvement whatsoever. And we have not been requested to be involved. We asked to be a part of the subcommittee, but that request was, in fact, denied.

speaker: katherinemaraman
text: Did you choose not to articulate any of the other reasons today?

speaker: gba
text: No, Your Honor, we have spent substantial time. And I've been informed that your honors have decided to promulgate the disciplinary rules. And those rules, in its final format, were posted to the website and provided to our bar on July 15. In fact, the entirety of the rules were not, in fact, posted. There is a significant appendix, which is approximately another 20 pages long, that was not provided as part of that process.

speaker: roberttorres
text: Are you referring to the sanctioned standards that were provided to the Bar Association when the draft rules were first sent out?

speaker: gba
text: Yes, when the draft rules were sent out. But when the final proposed rules for notice of this hearing was provided, those were not provided along with that. That's all I'm referencing.

speaker: roberttorres
text: But those standards haven't changed at all. So from what was originally provided to the bar, those standards were the standards that are set forth by the ABA committee and have been approved and in effect since February 1992. So there is nothing different in terms of the standards that are being recommended by the subcommittee for promulgation by the court as inclusion into the rules of the discipline.

speaker: gba
text: Yes, Your Honor, and that original document was approved by the American Bar Association in 1986. And one of the current concerns in terms of the objections of the bar, as I, on behalf of myself as an individual attorney in the bar membership, in addition to my being the president, have expressed that the type of bureaucracy and regulation imposed by the ABA and by the regulatory system is intended for a large mass attorney membership. Our membership is limited to 305. But out of respect for my membership and the bar, I have decided to withhold further commentary on the particular rules because I understand that there are various objections and various reasons that our 305 active member membership have already expressed to this court. And so any expression of further objection to the rules would essentially be my personal opinion.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: Any other questions or comments for President of the Lombard?

speaker: katherinemaraman
text: No, not for me.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: OK, I just want to thank you, Mr. Lai. I just want to say that we appreciate, first of all, I appreciate you commenting on the record. But a lot of the statements that you reference, in my mind, have been addressed through the journey that we have made together with the subcommittee as the clerk of court has outlined. But I appreciate your comments. So at this time, the court will recognize Attorney Mitch Thompson, who also signed up to present at this morning's hearing. So Attorney Thompson. All right, Mr. Thompson, we can see you. You're now in the virtual courtroom. And I see you have unmuted yourself. So you are recognized.

speaker: mitch
text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice and members of the court. I have previously submitted written comments in support of the proposed new rules. And I don't propose to reiterate those comments in length. I do think that the new rules bring the Guam disciplinary proceeding rules up to date in a number of ways. And the two most important ones are to make at least partially the disciplinary process much more open to the public. That is following the filing of formal charges. And that brings the disciplinary process for attorneys in line with the disciplinary process for all other Guam professionals, including Guam jurists. And I think that's a good thing. I'd also like to note that the new rules take the Guam Bar Association out of the disciplinary process. As I've noted previously, the ABA in their comment to rule two of their model rules stresses the importance of separating the state or local bar association from the disciplinary process. I think that given the events over the past few years, the wisdom of the ABA's comment has become apparent. And I ask the court to adopt the proposed new rules. I'd be happy to answer any questions should members of the court have any.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: Thank you. Justice Torres, do you have any questions for Mr. Thompson? You're muted, Justice Torres.

speaker: roberttorres
text: I have no questions for Mr. Thompson right now, Chief Justice. Justice Merriman?

speaker: katherinemaraman
text: I do not have any questions. Thank you.

speaker: roberttorres
text: All right. Thank you, attorney. Attorney Arreola is also asking to speak. So we just got a message.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: All right. OK. Thank you, Mr. Thompson. And you are now going to be placed back in the virtual gallery. And at this time, we will bring up Attorney Jay Arreola. After Mr. Arreola speaks, the only remaining speaker that I have, those who have submitted, would be Attorney Marian Wallace-Jones. And is she on the attendees' virtual gallery? She is there, Chief Justice. OK, thank you for that confirmation. All right, Attorney Jay Arreola, you are recognized.

speaker: arriola
text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, Justice Torres, and Justice Merriman. Speaking in my personal capacity as a lawyer who's practiced here for over 30 years, and together with the members of our firm at Arreola Law Firm, we express our strong opposition to the proposed disciplinary rules. Attorney Anita Arreola has submitted to the committee a number of objections, and reasons, and legal authorities on the rules. And we would submit on all of those objections. Justice Merriman is asking if the cost was the only reason members of the bar were opposing these rules. To answer Her Honor's question, no, Your Honor. The cost is not the only reason. The main reason we oppose these rules is because it is a significant and a substantial overhaul of our disciplinary system. There is no reason why we need to impose these rules. Just because these are adoption of the ADA model rules that have been in effect doesn't necessarily mean they apply to our Guam lawyers. We are a unified, integrated bar of less than 300 active members. The model rules apply mostly to the big states with thousands and thousands of lawyers subject to public discipline. These rules are simply an enactment of the ADA model rules just because. There is no problem that we have identified that these rules are meant to address. What is wrong? What is wrong with our current system that we have to adopt these new rules? In the preamble to the rules, there's no indication. We've suggested this several times even to the ADA committee that came out to Guam. What are we trying to achieve here? Are we not disciplining our lawyers? Are our lawyers just not complying with the rules? Is the caseload so high that we need to address these? And it's just simply disappointing. It's very disappointing having been a lawyer for so long here and having presented dozens of hours of work to this Supreme Court committee to engage the committee and ask that our concerns be addressed with these rules. All of the bar concerns have been disregarded, all of them. And so we would respectfully submit members of the court that the court should reject these rules and not implement them at this time. Thank you, Your Honor.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: Thank you, Mr. Areola. I'll ask you, Justice Torres, at the outset, do you have any comments or questions for Mr. Areola?

speaker: roberttorres
text: I don't have any particular questions directed to Mr. Areola. I would just note that as part of the process and in response to the Guam Bar Association's request, we actually agreed to bring out the American Bar Association Standing Committee on Professional Regulation, which went through the proposed rules that had been set forth by the committee, drafted by the committee after over two years of work. And they talked about and went through the strengths and description of the lawyer disciplinary system and the structure and made recommendations to the court. And many of the rules that we are adopting today are based on those recommendations and based on the report that was initiated by the Guam Bar Association.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: Justice Merriman?

speaker: katherinemaraman
text: I have no questions. Thank you. I would request, just for the record, if you could submit again the comments you're referring to from Attorney Anita Areola since you raised them.

speaker: arriola
text: Yes, Your Honor.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: I will. Thank you. I will. All right. Thank you, Attorney Areola, for taking the time and presenting your concerns and comments. At this time, the court will recognize Attorney Marian Wallischuk.

speaker: mariannewoloschuk
text: Good morning, Chief Justice and Justices of the Guam Supreme Court. Thank you very much for this opportunity to comment on the proposed rules. I'm here speaking as a member of the bar on behalf of myself. I want to address proposed Rule 16a, which makes public the matter when formal charges are filed unless there's a protective order obtained, which only covers testimony documents and records. At best, this is unclear. And at worst, it's unduly harsh and punitive. And I will explain that. But first, I want to give you my bottom line, just in case I run out of time to comment. The bottom line is, if you are determined to have this rule, I would ask that there be an allowance permission for a protective order to be obtained for the entire matter, not just for certain evidence before the hearing panel. And also, because it's the hearing panel that decides the protective order, I ask that there be allowed recourse to some impartial arbiter, like a court or a hearing officer, to review the hearing panel's decision. Because this is something that has the potential to really affect someone's life adversely. As you know, many attorneys run into ethics problems because of mental health or substance abuse problems. We do not, in Guam, have an ethics hotline. We do not have an advisory service. We do not have a lawyer's assistance program. We don't have a bar journal where you can write in and ask for advice or where certain opinions are published. When you look at the ABA website, they will note that 50 states and the District of Columbia and the US Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico all have lawyer's assistance programs. We alone, with maybe the CNMI and the Panama Canal Zone, are the only ones who don't have a lawyer's assistance program. And I believe this rule is very harsh to someone when they're already down. If you compare this to the imposition of criminal charges, both of these events have great potential to affect people's lives. But when there's criminal charges being imposed, you have the police involved, the prosecutors, magistrate judge, a grand jury. There are at least 20 people involved. Under Rule 3, the investigative panel quorum is four people. So four people could make a decision that could irreparably harm an attorney's life. So in conclusion, I'm asking that you amend this rule because our jurisdiction is very different from everybody else's to allow the entire matter to be sealed and for there to be recourse to an impartial arbiter. Thank you.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: Thank you, Ms. Wallischuk. Although your oral presentation is part of the record and we have transcripts, I would request that if you could reduce your presentation to writing and submit that with the court, that would be very helpful for the court to make sure that we properly understand and address if we haven't already your concerns.

speaker: mariannewoloschuk
text: I will do that, Your Honor. Thank you.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: And if you just hold on and let me ask if Justice Torres has any comments or questions for Ms. Wallischuk.

speaker: roberttorres
text: I just have a brief comment, Chief Justice, and that is Ms. Wallischuk, I agree with you that we do need a lawyer assistance program. And I think it's important that the Guam Bar take the initiative. And I think all members of the court would support wholeheartedly any efforts to try to establish a lawyer assistance program on Guam.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: And Justice Merriman, do you have any questions or comments for Ms. Wallischuk?

speaker: katherinemaraman
text: If I may, yes. Subsection B of Rule 16 provides that if it's a disability type of proceeding, that all the matters remain confidential. What type of case you envision would not, if someone has a disability, how that would become public.

speaker: mariannewoloschuk
text: And it's just the way the rule is written, Your Honor. When you look at 16A and 16E, it says testimony, records, and documents. It doesn't say the entire matter. I think it needs to be clear so that the entire matter can be sealed. Also, there's no provision for recourse to an impartial arbiter once the hearing panel makes a decision.

speaker: katherinemaraman
text: So how do you construe that phrase, unless a protective order is obtained? Wouldn't that come from a court?

speaker: mariannewoloschuk
text: I think it's the rule provides that the hearing panel will decide whether there is a protective order.

speaker: katherinemaraman

speaker: mariannewoloschuk
text: Thank you, Your Honor. I'll do that.

speaker: katherinemaraman

speaker: philipcarbullido
